title: Rabbi Gamliel (IV)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: In Hyman’s account, his father Rabbi Yehudah Nesia was the last Patriarch to hold both patriarchal authority and the headship of the academy. When he died, the patriarchate was divided in two. The academy of Tzippori had not yet been dissolved. Hyman next describes Rabbi Oshaya going to Caesarea in his old age and founding his academy there, Rabbi Yannai in the town of Akhbara, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in Lod. Rabbi Yehudah Nesia died about the year 542 of the Seleucid era (lishtarot), having served as Patriarch nearly thirty years. His son Rabbi Gamliel was not great either in Torah or in wisdom like his fathers, and could not be the captain and head of the generation. Within a few years Rabbi Yochanan went and founded his great academy in Tiberias; therefore we find this Rabbi Gamliel almost nowhere, except in Jerusalem Talmud Challah 4:4, where Rabban Gamliel Berabbi (so all the Patriarchs are called in the Jerusalem Talmud) wished to institute demai in Syria and Rabbi Hoshaya did not let him. Hyman concludes from this that he did not reach his fathers’ level. Secondly, his patriarchate did not last long — not that he died young, but because his father Rabbi Yehudah Nesia had a long patriarchate. Therefore no halakhah of his is mentioned, nor any general enactment, since the Sanhedrin and its authority had been abolished and the honor of the Torah was given to the heads of the academies; only the honor of the patriarchate — such as the appointment of judges and the intercalation of the year — remained with the Patriarchs. In his place sat Rabbi Yehudah Nesia the second, who was Rabbi Yochanan’s student.

notes.text: טרם נתבטלה is rendered had not yet been dissolved; reversing it to already dissolved would remove the supplied negation. The supplied phrase says had not yet been dissolved, although the following causal account is awkward; retain that negation and hold the intended transition pending a better Hyman witness. Saved Guggenheimer Challah4:4 supports Syria, בסוריא, versus supplied בסורא, and benRabbi versus supplied beRabbi. Hyman’s542Seleucid date, thirty-year patriarchate, decline assessment and institutional history remain his account, without a modern historical proof claim.

Hyman’s printed entry (vol. I, p. 320) and the Wikisource transcription both read טרם נתבטלה, rendered here “had not yet been dissolved.” The Hebrew links this statement to the account of Rabbi Oshaya with כי. The connection is unclear. The translation keeps the order and the negative wording.

In the consulted edition of Jerusalem Talmud Challah 4:4:5, the text says בן רבי (“the son of Rebbi”) and בסוריא (“in Syria”). Hyman’s printed entry has ברבי and בסורא. In his separate entry for Gamliel (III), Hyman argues that Gamliel (IV) is the figure in Challah. The exchange he cites in Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 1:11 records Rabbi Hoshaya asking Yehudah Nesia what he heard from his father. It leaves the father unnamed.
